origin_region: Miyazaki · Takachiho and Gokase; Kumamoto; Saga · Ureshino
cultivar: Yabukita, Minekaori, Takachiho (a local cultivar), seed-grown zairai bushes
processing: Fresh leaf is fired in a hot pan or heated rotating drum (traditionally starting around 300 °C) instead of being steamed, then rolled and dried, with a final pan roast that gives the toasty 'kama-ka' aroma; the leaf ends up curled rather than needle-shaped.
harvest_season: First flush in late April–May, later than the lowlands because the growing areas are in the mountains; some second-flush lots.
appearance_dry: Twisted, curled olive-green leaves with a dull, matte surface and the occasional yellow-green tip, looking more Chinese than Japanese.
appearance_liquor: Clear, bright gold-yellow rather than green.
taste_profile: Toasty, nutty pan aroma with a light, clean body, sweet chestnut notes and a crisp finish; little of the seaweed umami of steamed tea.

brewing.notes: Hotter than sencha (80–90 °C) to lift the roasted aroma; it is far more forgiving of timing and heat. A kyusu or a gaiwan both work, and it cold-brews bright and clean.

vintage_note: A small-production tea sold by the current year's harvest, almost always first flush, by family farms in Miyazaki, Kumamoto and Saga, often labelled with the village (Takachiho, Gokase) and sometimes the cultivar. Fresh lots appear in May; it holds its aroma a little better than steamed tea but is still best within the year.
description:
Kamairicha is Japan's pan-fired green tea, the rare exception to steaming. It is made in the mountains of Miyazaki (Takachiho and Gokase above all), in Kumamoto and around Ureshino in Saga, and it accounts for only a small fraction of the country's output. The pan-firing method came to Kyushu from China long before the steamed sencha process was developed in the eighteenth century, so in a sense this is the older Japanese green tea.

Fresh leaf goes into a hot pan or a heated rotating drum, traditionally at around 300 °C to begin with, where it is tossed until the enzymes are killed and the leaf goes limp; it is then rolled and dried, and finished with a further pan roast. No steam means a clear, golden cup rather than a green one, and the hot metal gives the toasty 'kama-ka' aroma that is the whole point. The leaf stays curled and twisted, closer in look to a Chinese green than to sencha.

It is the easiest Japanese green tea to brew. Water at 80–90 °C, 5 g for 150 ml, a minute for the first steep and shorter for the second, and it gives a light, clean cup with toasted nut, a sweet chestnut note, a little grass and a crisp finish, with almost none of the seaweed umami of steamed tea. It shrugs off slightly hot water and slightly long steeps, and a gaiwan works as well as a kyusu. Cold-brewed it is bright and refreshing.

It comes from small family farms and is sold by the current year's first flush, often with the village on the label and sometimes the cultivar; Takachiho and Gokase are the names to look for, and 'kama-guri' on a Saga tea means the same pan-fired, curly style. It costs a little more than lowland sencha because the mountain yields are low and the work is still partly by hand. Store it like any green tea, although it holds its aroma a little longer than steamed sencha does.

It is the natural bridge for anyone who drinks Chinese greens such as Longjing and wants to try Japan without the steamed flavour.
